title: Saw a 45-degree mitre through a picture-frame moulding in a mitre box
instruction: Saw the moulding right through at its pencil line in the mitre box's 45-degree slot, with the moulding against the box's back fence, so the cut is a true 45-degree mitre (within half a degree). Leave the saw standing back in its rest, the cut moulding lying on the table in front of the box and both arms back where they started.
context: Sawing a piece of wood by hand is one of the most familiar manual jobs there is, and the mitre box is how it is done at home when the cut must be angled: making a picture frame, or fitting a skirting board or trim round a corner. A beech mitre box and a small backsaw cost $56 together ($14.99 and $40.99, the pair named in the README). Watching a few seconds of one hand holding the moulding to the box's fence while the other saws, anyone sees what is being done. The box sets the saw's angle, but the cut is only as true as that hold: each stroke drags a moulding nobody holds along the box, and a mitre half a degree off already opens a gap in the frame's corner.
setup: A table in front of two arms (bases 61 cm apart), seen by one overhead camera and a camera on each wrist. Distances are measured forward from the line between the arm bases and sideways from the midpoint between them. (1) A beech mitre box (Pinie, 245 x 103 x 60 mm), fixed: an 18 mm birch-ply base from 29.6 to 39.9 cm forward and from 15 cm right to 9.5 cm left of the centre line, with a front wall and a back fence of 19 mm beech standing 41 mm over it either side of a 65 mm wide channel (the back fence's face 38 cm forward). Saw slots 2.5 mm wide, their top 8 mm chamfered out to 1 cm, cut through both walls: two at 45 degrees crossing the channel's middle 5 cm right of the centre line, and one at 90 degrees 3 cm left of it. Butted to the box's left end, a support block of the same ply runs on to 28 cm left, and a 6 mm MDF packing strip lies along the channel's floor and on over the block. (2) On the table in front of the box, a 34 cm length of 26 x 23 mm black picture-frame moulding (pine or fir, 98.5 g) with a gold lip along its front edge, lying along the box 21.5 cm forward, from 8.1 cm right to 26.0 cm left of the centre line; a white pencil line crosses its top at 45 degrees 5 cm from its right end. (3) To the right, a 10-inch gents saw (160 g): a steel blade 255 mm long with 20 teeth per inch, 40 mm deep under a brass back, with a turned walnut handle (133 mm) in line with it, standing teeth down in a beech saw rest (two V-blocks under the blade and a V-cradle under the handle) 21 cm right of the centre line, the blade running forward from 25.3 to 50.8 cm, the handle reaching back toward the arms. The layout is the same in every trial, as in the screenshot.
scoring: Judged from the whole trial. The moulding is at the mark when its pencil line lies within 1 cm of the 45-degree slot along the box, its back face within 6 mm of the fence, turned less than 4 degrees and lying on the packing strip; it has been laid there once it stays so for 0.5 s. The cut is true when every stroke that deepened it ran at 45 degrees to the moulding's back edge within 0.5 degree: a mitre 0.5 degree off leaves its joint with a true one open by up to 36.8 mm (the cut's length across the 26 mm moulding) x tan 0.5 degree = 0.32 mm. The saw is back in its rest when it stands within 2 cm of where it started, within 1.2 cm of its height and turned less than 10 degrees from it; the cut moulding is out on the table when it lies on the table in front of the box's base. 1.0: cut through and true, the saw back in its rest, the cut moulding out on the table and both arms back where they started (each gripper's fingertip centre within 5 cm of its start), at the end; 0.75: cut through and true; 0.5: a kerf at least 11.5 mm deep (half the moulding's 23 mm height), or a cut through that is not true; 0.25: the moulding laid at the mark; else 0.0. In a real trial the cut is measured afterwards and counts only within 1 cm of the pencil line; the mark and the end state are judged from the video. True: a 45-degree mitre square held to the kept piece's back edge, its blade along the cut face across the top; a 0.33 mm (0.013 in) feeler gauge must not enter between them anywhere (0.33 mm over 36.8 mm is 0.51 degree). Kerf depth: a caliper's depth rod from the top face to the deepest point of the kerf. Cut through: the offcut free along the kerf, sawn over the full height and width; an offcut snapped or torn off with uncut fibres is not cut through, and the kerf's sawn depth scores instead. In simulation the wood is not cut (see fidelity): the saw saws only while it moves forward along the 45-degree slot (within 9 mm of its line, turned within 8 and leaning within 12 degrees of it), the moulding lies at the mark, and its teeth press on the bottom of the cut with at least 1.5 N (PhysX contact force) at both ends of a control step. A stroke is 3 cm of such sawing in one push against a mean resistance of at least 3.5 N (the measured friction opposing the saw: at least 0.105 J of work done against the cut), the moulding moving no more than 4 mm; a saw moved above the cut without touching it saws nothing. Each stroke deepens the cut 3 mm, so four (12 mm) earn 0.5 and the eighth (24 mm) frees the offcut. A stroke's angle is the blade's angle to the moulding's back edge, read from the two parts' poses and averaged over its sawing. The trial ends at the run limit, or once the full score has held for 1 s with the saw and both pieces of the moulding still.
reset_notes: Lay a fresh moulding (a 34 cm length with its pencil line) on the table in front of the box; brush the sawdust off the box, the strip and the table; stand the saw back in its rest, teeth down, handle toward the arms, and only then take its blade guard off, with both arms at home. Renew the packing strip once its kerf is about 5 mm deep.
fidelity: Rigid-body simulation (Isaac Sim 6.1, PhysX, 20 Hz control). The wood is not cut: the teeth ride on a hidden plate in the moulding that steps down 3 mm per stroke (8 free the offcut); real trials measure the kerf. A stroke needs real contact (1.5 N) and 3.5 N mean friction against the saw over 3 cm; simulated teeth need more feed than real ones for it. Blade 2 mm thick (real 0.56), 0.5 mm slot play, slot lead-in chamfers the real box lacks. Box fixed. Cameras 1280 x 704 (Dream-1 sees 320 x 176).
